items.label: ISS smoke detectors
items.value: Photoelectric smoke detectors in each module, as spot or duct monitors
items.quote: segments of the International Space Station (ISS) will have one or more detector units in each module that sense smoke through photoelectric light-beam obscuration and scattering

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

items.label: Confirm with gas sensing
items.value: Combined CO/CO₂ sensing can tell flaming from non-flaming events
items.quote: combined CO/CO 2 detectors are shown in ground tests to discriminate among non-flaming fires, flaming fires, and non-fire events.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

items.label: Don't rely on seeing flames
items.value: Low-flow microgravity flames can be nearly invisible; FLEX cool flames kept 'burning' after the visible flame went out
items.quote: FLEX ... led to the discovery of a type of cool flame, where the fuel continued “burning” under certain conditions after extinction of the visible flame.

source.label: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office

items.label: Orion
items.value: Orion's smoke detector is adapted from a mature commercial-aircraft design
items.quote: The smoke detector described in this paper is an adaptation of a mature commercial aircraft design for manned spaceflight.

source.label: Smoke Detection for the Orion Crew Exploration Vehicle (2009, NTRS 20090020655)

items.label: First response
items.value: Isolate the zone: remove power and air circulation
items.quote: Upon a verified fire alarm, the automated or manual crew response is to isolate the affected zone, removing power and local or general air circulation.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

items.label: Necessary, not sufficient
items.value: Stopping airflow may not put out every fire (a candle on Mir burned for minutes)
items.quote: removal of air flow upon fire detection is a necessary response, but it is not always sufficient for control of the incipient fire.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

items.label: Saffire lesson
items.value: Charring or bubbling materials may not self-extinguish quickly in still air
items.quote: Extinguishment of thin charring fuels at increased oxygen cannot be assumed to occur rapidly in quiescent conditions.

source.label: Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

items.label: Saffire lesson
items.value: A small residual flow can sometimes help extinction
items.quote: In some circumstances, reducing air flow to a small value rather than quiescent conditions may be useful to disperse fuel vapor and help cool the material to enable extinction

source.label: Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

items.label: ISS extinguishers
items.value: CO₂ in the US segment, Columbus and Kibo; water foam in the Russian segment
items.quote: The International Space Station presently uses two different types of fire extinguishers: a water foam extinguisher in the Russian Segment, and a carbon dioxide extinguisher in the US Segment and Columbus and Kibo pressurized elements.

source.label: Development of the ISS Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (2011, NTRS 20110012300)

items.label: Why water mist
items.value: Fine water mist avoids filling the cabin with CO₂ and low-O₂ air
items.quote: Fine Water Mist extinguishes a fire without creating a large volume of air with reduced oxygen and elevated CO2.

source.label: Development of the ISS Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (2011, NTRS 20110012300)

items.label: Crew breathing
items.value: Fire-response respirator cartridge rated up to 90 min; it does not filter CO₂
items.quote: It is qualified to provide up to 90 minutes of capability ... The fire response respirator cartridge does not filter carbon dioxide (CO2)

source.label: Development of the ISS Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (2011, NTRS 20110012300)

items.label: Orion
items.value: Orion uses a water-spray portable extinguisher
items.quote: The Orion crew capsule will utilize a different PFE technology from ISS (water spray rather than water mist)

source.label: Orion Portable Fire Extinguisher Performance Testing ... (2018, NTRS 20180005251)

items.label: Depressurization
items.value: If used, drop the pressure fast
items.quote: if a fire is to be controlled by depressurization, the pressure in the affected module should be decreased rapidly

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

items.label: Standard test
items.value: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1: upward burning in the worst expected atmosphere
items.quote: The method is a pass/fail upward flame propagation test conducted in the most severe flaming combustion environment (oxygen concentration, pressure) expected in the spacecraft

source.label: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

items.label: Low-g margin
items.value: Some materials burn at lower O₂ in low g than in 1 g
items.quote: 1g flammability limits are generally not conservative for these materials as evidenced by the negative ∆O2%, by up to -5.75% oxygen.

source.label: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

items.label: Higher O₂ habitats
items.value: Fire-safe materials get harder to find as O₂ rises
items.quote: Fire safe materials become increasingly difficult to find as the oxygen concentration increases.

source.label: Ferkul et al. (2026) Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, LPSC presentation (NTRS 20260001966)

items.label: Saffire lesson
items.value: Thick-fuel growth in low g differs from Test 1
items.quote: Thick fuel flame growth was found to be dissimilar from that seen in NASA STD 6001 Test 1. This does not invalidate the test but does affect the interpretation of the test results

source.label: Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

items.label: Re-ignition
items.value: Hot embers can re-ignite if fresh air returns too early
items.quote: Since burned material remains hot in the non-convective environment, embers may reignite if prematurely exposed to fresh air.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

items.label: Deflagration risk
items.value: Overheated materials in still zones can build up fuel vapour
items.quote: Overheated materials in quiescent conditions or in low-flow zones in low gravity can produce stratified fuel mixtures that can result in dramatic deflagrations during ignition.

source.label: Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

items.label: Flame jumps
items.value: A flame jumped a 4.5 cm gap to a warmed PMMA surface
items.quote: In one case, a flame was seen to jump a 4.5 cm gap to ignite a previously warmed PMMA surface.

source.label: Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

items.label: Large fire impact
items.value: Saffire fires up to 10 kW did not push average vehicle conditions to unacceptable levels
items.quote: despite having heat release rates up to 10 kW, the average vehicle conditions did not rise to unacceptable levels.

source.label: Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

items.label: Most flammable band
items.value: Flammability and spread rate peak between about 0.15 and 0.4 g
items.quote: the fuels exhibit a maximum in their flammability behavior in the partial-gravity range.

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

items.label: New hazards
items.value: Dormancy, higher O₂, partial gravity and surface dust
items.quote: extended durations, dormancy intervals, increased oxygen concentrations, partial gravity conditions and the presence of surface dust. All of these changes can have significant impacts on fire safety system design and operations.

source.label: Spacecraft Fire Safety Technology Development Plan for Exploration Missions (NTRS 20205000063)

items.label: Self-reliance
items.value: Less suppressant, delayed contact with Earth
items.quote: Stores of suppressant and atmospheric diluents are more limited, long missions imply more accumulated wastes and possible relaxation of crew vigilance

source.label: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
